article.paragraph 1: A quiet teen with tragic past suspected in fatal northern Quebec stabbings
article.paragraph 2: Police say Illutak Anautak, 19, stabbed 3 people to death before being fatally shot by officer
article.paragraph 3: The teen shot and killed by police following three fatal stabbings in a northern Quebec community on the weekend was dealing with a number of tragic events from his past, including the slaying of his mother and the suicide of his brother.
article.paragraph 4: Illutak Anautak, 19, who was described by friends and family as quiet young man with an easy smile, was identified by local officials as the man shot dead by police in the Inuit village of Akulivik after three break-ins during which five people were stabbed early Saturday morning.
article.paragraph 5: The dead were identified as Anautak's uncle, Lucassie Anautak, a cousin who was about 10 years old, and Eli Qinuajuak, his aunt's partner, three local officials confirmed to CBC News.
article.paragraph 6: Two others were taken to hospital with injuries. Investigators said Sunday evening that they are no longer listed as being in critical condition.
article.paragraph 7: Anautak's mother was killed by her boyfriend in 2014, friends say, while an older brother took his own life eight or nine years ago.
article.paragraph 8: Randy McLeod, Anautak's former teacher at the local school, described Anautak as a "very nice, extremely respectful" student. In 2011, Anautak was among a group of students who joined McLeod on an educational trip to Montreal.
article.paragraph 9: At the same time, McLeod said, the young man was "dealing with a lot of personal things and perhaps there wasn't any support."
article.paragraph 10: "He was dealing with a lot of trauma; I guess that maybe was too much," said McLeod, who is on leave from his position at the school.
article.paragraph 11: "I don't know what the trigger was, what created the situation. Obviously I wasn't there."
article.paragraph 12: McLeod worries that even if Anautak had sought help, the mental health resources wouldn't have been available.
article.paragraph 13: "You need that kind of thing to be available to you in those moments, not, 'Ok, we'll get a counsellor flown here in a couple weeks to speak in another language,'" he said.
article.paragraph 14: Despite his troubles, though, friends say Anautak rarely showed signs of anger.
article.paragraph 15: He was passionate about hockey — he played goalie and volunteered as a coach in the community — and posted photos on his Facebook page in appreciation of his hometown.
article.paragraph 16: In a post accompanying a photo just last month, he wrote, "Akulivik always the best!"
article.paragraph 17: He had three younger siblings and was "like a father to them," said Rebecca Tukalak, one of his closest friends.
article.paragraph 18: He was "just always smiling and a funny guy," she said in an interview on Facebook messenger, adding that he never showed signs of aggression.
article.paragraph 20: Still, Anautuk struggled to cope with the death of his mother.
article.paragraph 21: He was known in Akulivik, a village of about 600, as a "quiet person," said his uncle and a local councillor, Eli Aullaluk.
article.paragraph 22: "This is not normal. I feel sorry for all the people in this community. Our prayers go them all," he said.
article.paragraph 23: In 2015, in a rare display of emotion on social media, Anautuk wrote, "I finally get it mom, I miss you so much."
article.paragraph 24: Tukalak, who lives in Puvirnituq, a remote community further south, said she last saw Anautuk in May, and he didn't seem like himself.
article.paragraph 25: "He was really weird and was talking really low. I think that was a goodbye," she said.
article.paragraph 26: Her takeaway, she said, is that even the "most nice and quiet people explode one day, so it is really important to express truest feelings."
